content: Patched (Ptc) is a highly conserved 12-pass transmembrane protein receptor that serves as a critical negative regulator in the Hedgehog signaling pathway, functioning in both insects and vertebrates. This protein plays an indispensable role during embryogenesis, particularly in ensuring proper segmentation in Drosophila embryos. Mutations in the patched gene can result in embryonic lethality. Patched acts as the receptor for the Hedgehog protein and regulates its spatial distribution. This regulation is partially achieved through the endocytosis of Hedgehog protein bound to Patched, which is subsequently directed to lysosomes for degradation. Discovery The initial mutations in the patched (ptc) gene were identified in the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster by Nobel Laureates Eric F. Wieschaus and Christiane Nüsslein-Volhard, along with their colleagues. The gene was independently cloned in 1989 by Joan Hooper in the laboratory of Matthew P. Scott, as well as by Philip Ingham and his collaborators. Role in Hedgehog Signaling Patched is a key component of a negative feedback mechanism within the Hedgehog signaling pathway. This feedback system helps establish the spatial gradient of signaling activity across tissues. In the absence of Hedgehog, low levels of Patched are sufficient to suppress the activity of the signal transduction pathway. When Hedgehog is present, its cholesterol moiety binds to the sterol-sensing domain of Patched, which in turn inhibits the activity of Smoothened, a G protein-coupled receptor. Smoothened is predominantly stored in membrane-bound vesicles within the cell and is mobilized to the cell surface upon Hedgehog stimulation. The presence of Smoothened on the cell membrane is essential for the activation of the Hedgehog signaling pathway. Hedgehog signaling also induces the transcription of the patched gene, leading to the accumulation of Patched protein, which subsequently limits signaling through Smoothened. Recent studies have highlighted the role of the cilium in the intracellular trafficking of Hedgehog signaling components in vertebrate cells. Role in Disease Mutations in the patched protein have been implicated in several cancers, including basal cell carcinoma, medulloblastoma, and rhabdomyosarcoma. Hereditary mutations in the human homolog of patched, PTCH1, are responsible for autosomal dominant Gorlin syndrome. This syndrome is characterized by tissue overgrowth and a predisposition to cancers such as basal cell carcinoma and medulloblastoma. Similarly, mice with mutations in the mouse PTCH1 gene develop medulloblastoma, mirroring the human condition.
